name: Seder · The Jewish Learning Academy — Foundational Skill Graph
principle: Skills are the product; content is the vehicle. Each skill is a transferable reading capability that a learner can carry from one genre of the Jewish canon to another. Foundational-skill IDs (prefixed fnd-) are deliberately separate from content-unit IDs so that any source can teach any skill.

promise.core: Become someone who can learn the Jewish canon.
promise.emotional: Open your letter in the scroll.

masteryScale.emerging: can make the move with support
masteryScale.secure: can make the move unaided in two familiar genres
masteryScale.transfer: can make the move in an unfamiliar source or a genre it was not practiced in

layers.title: Orientation
layers.intent: Identify what a source is, where you are on the page, who is speaking, and whether it is asking a question.

layers.title: Text signals
layers.intent: Recognize high-frequency words, connectors, quotation, and attribution cues before reaching for a full translation.

layers.title: Source roles
layers.intent: Distinguish text from translation and commentary, and question from answer, example, and ruling.

layers.title: Case mapping
layers.intent: Identify who acts, what happens, what is uncertain, and what factor changes the outcome.

layers.title: Argument tracking
layers.intent: Follow claim, evidence, objection, response, and unresolved tension.

layers.title: Comparison
layers.intent: Place two sources side by side and name shared question, divergence, and scope.

layers.title: Context
layers.intent: Ask when, where, by whom, and for what community a source was formed, and what evidence it can give.

layers.title: Practice & responsibility
layers.intent: Distinguish learning a source from receiving personal or practical guidance; hold disagreement and name limits.

layers.title: Independent reading
layers.intent: Make a supported first pass through an unfamiliar short source and carry a move across genres.

layers.title: Learning agency
layers.intent: Ask a good question, use a source tool, record uncertainty, and choose the next study move.

graduationContract.means: The learner has demonstrated the foundational skill set across at least three source genres, including at least one unfamiliar source, and can choose a responsible next study move on their own.
graduationContract.doesNotMean: The learner has completed the Shas or mastered any single subject.
produces: a portfolio of source maps and transfer evidence
a recommended set of next academies or electives

durabilityTiers.foundation: Review at 1, 3, 7, and 21 days; refresh whenever a later skill depends on it.
durabilityTiers.core: Review at 3, 10, and 30 days; refresh on first use inside a new genre.
durabilityTiers.transfer: Review at 7 and 30 days; confirmed only by success in an unseen source.

skills.title: Tell what kind of text you are looking at
skills.statement: You can say whether a source is Torah, Mishnah, Gemara, commentary, a code, or a prayer.
skills.teachingMove: Show three short sources side by side and name the tell-tale shape of each genre before reading a word for meaning.
checks: Given an unlabeled snippet, name its genre and one feature that gave it away.
skills.transfer: Label the genre of a snippet from a genre not shown in the lesson.
skills.repair: Return to the labeled gallery of genre shapes and match the snippet to the closest one.

skills.title: Find the main text and what surrounds it
skills.statement: You can locate the primary text on a page and tell it apart from what is wrapped around it.
skills.teachingMove: Point to the center column and trace outward, naming each ring as 'the text' or 'talk about the text'.
checks: Circle the primary text on a page image and mark one surrounding layer.
skills.transfer: Do the same on a siddur page with commentary you have not seen.
skills.repair: Ask one question: which block would still make sense if everything around it were removed?

skills.title: Identify who is speaking
skills.statement: You can tell who is speaking or being quoted in a source.
skills.teachingMove: Underline names and 'said' words first; treat everything after them as that voice until the next name.
checks: Attribute two lines of a passage to the right speaker.
skills.transfer: Track the speakers in a short narrative from Torah.
skills.repair: Read only the names in order and retell the passage as a conversation.

skills.title: Find where one idea starts and stops
skills.statement: You can mark where a single unit of thought begins and ends.
skills.teachingMove: Look for the seams: a new name, a new question, a new case, or a blank in the flow.
checks: Split a passage into its units and name the seam for each split.
skills.transfer: Segment a halakhic paragraph you have not read before.
skills.repair: Read aloud and mark every place you naturally pause for breath or topic.

skills.title: Notice when a source is asking, not telling
skills.statement: You can tell whether a line is asking a question or stating something.
skills.teachingMove: Ask of each line: does this expect an answer? Mark it Q or S before translating.
checks: Label three lines as question or statement.
skills.transfer: Find the question inside a philosophical passage.
skills.repair: Say the line out loud with question intonation and see whether it wants a reply.

skills.title: Recognize a bank of high-frequency words
skills.statement: You can sight-read a growing bank of common Hebrew and Aramaic words without stopping to decode.
skills.teachingMove: Build and rehearse a small word wall of the highest-frequency words, met again in every new source.
checks: Recognize ten bank words on sight in a fresh passage.
skills.transfer: Spot the same words inside a prayer you have not studied.
skills.repair: Return to the word wall and re-meet the missed words in a sentence you already know.

skills.title: Recognize question-signal words
skills.statement: You can spot the words that flag a question and predict what kind of answer they want.
skills.teachingMove: Learn a short set of question particles and pair each with the shape of answer it invites.
checks: Given a question word, predict whether the answer will be a reason, a case, or a source.
skills.transfer: Predict the answer shape for a question in an unseen sugya.
skills.repair: Match the question word to the example on the particle card and reread.

skills.title: Recognize argument connectors
skills.statement: You can recognize the small words that mean 'therefore', 'but', 'as it says', and 'this teaches'.
skills.teachingMove: Highlight connectors in one color; read only the connectors to feel the shape of the argument.
checks: Classify three connectors as adding, opposing, or citing.
skills.transfer: Trace the connectors through a Mussar passage you have not seen.
skills.repair: Replace each connector with a plain English word and reread the flow.

skills.title: Notice when a source quotes another source
skills.statement: You can tell when a source is bringing in another text rather than speaking in its own voice.
skills.teachingMove: Learn the citation formulas; when one appears, bracket the quoted words as borrowed.
checks: Bracket the quoted material in a short passage and name its source type.
skills.transfer: Find the quotation inside a piece of Chassidut you have not read.
skills.repair: Look only for the citation formula, then read the words immediately after it.

skills.title: Recognize attribution formulas
skills.statement: You can recognize the standard 'Rabbi X said' patterns that assign a statement to a voice.
skills.teachingMove: Collect the attribution formulas as a family; each one hands the next words to a named voice.
checks: Mark every attribution in a passage and list the voices in order.
skills.transfer: Do the same in a source from a tractate you have not studied.
skills.repair: Read only the attributions aloud and reconstruct who said what.

skills.title: Tell primary text from commentary
skills.statement: You can separate a primary text from a comment written about it.
skills.teachingMove: Ask which text could stand alone and which only exists to explain another; label accordingly.
checks: Given two blocks, say which is the source and which is the commentary, with a reason.
skills.transfer: Separate text from commentary on a halakhic page you have not seen.
skills.repair: Cover the commentary and check that the primary text still reads as a whole.

skills.title: Notice where a translation makes a choice
skills.statement: You can see where a translation adds, drops, or chooses a meaning the original leaves open.
skills.teachingMove: Compare two translations of one phrase; mark the word where they part ways and ask why.
checks: Point to one word where a translation committed to a choice.
skills.transfer: Find a translation choice in a piece of Jewish thought you have not studied.
skills.repair: Look up the single disputed word and list two meanings it can carry.

skills.title: Label question, answer, or restatement
skills.statement: You can label a line as a question, an answer, or a restatement of what came before.
skills.teachingMove: Tag each line Q, A, or R; a passage should read as a chain of these tags.
checks: Tag four consecutive lines and defend one tag.
skills.transfer: Tag the moves in an unseen short sugya.
skills.repair: For each line ask: is this new pressure, a reply, or the same point again?

skills.title: Recognize a worked example
skills.statement: You can tell when a source drops into a concrete case to make a point.

sourceContexts.ref: Orchot Tzaddikim, a worked case of a middah

skills.teachingMove: When the text turns to 'someone who...', treat it as a test case for the rule just stated.
checks: Point to the example and state the rule it is testing.
skills.transfer: Find the illustrative case in a Mussar teaching you have not read.
skills.repair: Ask: is this the rule, or a story that shows the rule?

skills.title: Distinguish a ruling from a discussion
skills.statement: You can tell a settled ruling from open discussion around it.
skills.teachingMove: Ask whether the text decides or explores; a decision closes options, a discussion opens them.
checks: Label a passage as ruling or discussion and cite the deciding word.
skills.transfer: Make the same call on an unseen halakhic paragraph.
skills.repair: Ask whether a reader is left with one option or several.

skills.title: Identify who acts
skills.statement: You can name who is acting in a case and what they do.
skills.teachingMove: List the actors as a cast, then attach one verb to each.
checks: List every actor in a case and one thing each does.
skills.transfer: Do the same for an unseen narrative from history material.
skills.repair: Reread and circle every person or party before reading for meaning.

skills.title: State what happens in plain language
skills.statement: You can restate the situation of a case in ordinary words.
skills.teachingMove: Tell the case as a one-sentence story before touching the legal or conceptual question.
checks: Give a one-sentence plain-language summary of a case.
skills.transfer: Summarize an unseen case from a different tractate.
skills.repair: Answer only: who, did what, to whom?

skills.title: Name what is uncertain
skills.statement: You can name the point of uncertainty or dispute at the heart of a case.
skills.teachingMove: Ask what the case would need in order to be decided; the missing thing is the uncertainty.
checks: State the open question a case turns on.
skills.transfer: Find the uncertainty in an unseen halakhic case.
skills.repair: Ask: what are the two things this could be, and why is it not obvious?

skills.title: Find the factor that changes the outcome
skills.statement: You can identify the detail that would change how a case comes out.
skills.teachingMove: Change one detail of the case out loud and watch whether the ruling moves; the mover is the key factor.
checks: Name one factor that, if changed, would flip the outcome.
skills.transfer: Identify the deciding factor in an unseen case.
skills.repair: List the details of the case and test them one at a time.

skills.title: Restate a case in your own words
skills.statement: You can retell a case accurately without leaning on its original wording.
skills.teachingMove: Close the text and retell it; then reopen and check what you dropped or changed.
checks: Retell a case from memory and mark any detail you missed.
skills.transfer: Retell an unseen short passage from another genre.
skills.repair: Retell just the first half, check it, then add the rest.

skills.title: Classify the case into a category
skills.statement: You can name the legal or conceptual category a case falls under and why.

sourceContexts.ref: Mishnah Bava Kamma 1:1 (the primary categories of damage)
Rambam, Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:1 (avot and toladot)
Orchot Tzaddikim (naming the middah a deed belongs to)

skills.teachingMove: Ask what named category this case is an instance of; sort the particular under the general before reasoning further.
checks: Given a case, name the category it belongs to and one feature that places it there.
skills.transfer: Classify an unseen case from a genre you did not practice.
skills.repair: List the candidate categories and test the case against each one's defining feature.

skills.title: Follow the order of a procedure
skills.statement: You can put the steps of a procedure in order and say why the order matters.

sourceContexts.ref: Yoma 33a (the fixed order of the daily Temple service)
The order of the weekday Amidah blessings
Rambam, Hilchot Tefillin 4 (the sequence of donning tefillin)

skills.teachingMove: Number the steps as an ordered list, then ask which steps could not swap places without breaking the procedure.
checks: Put the steps of a procedure in order and flag one step whose position is fixed.
skills.transfer: Order the steps of an unfamiliar procedure from another genre.
skills.repair: Retell the procedure as 'first…, then…, then…' and check each 'then' against the source.

skills.title: Identify who is obligated and who is exempt
skills.statement: You can say who a rule obligates, who it exempts, and on what ground.

sourceContexts.ref: Rambam, Hilchot Berakhot 1 (obligation and exemption in blessings)
Kiddushin 29a (a father's and the community's obligations)

skills.teachingMove: For each party in the case ask: obligated, exempt, or forbidden — and what fact decides it.
checks: Name who is obligated and who is exempt in a case, with the deciding ground for each.
skills.transfer: Sort obligation and exemption in an unseen case from another genre.
skills.repair: List the parties, attach 'must / need not / may not' to each, and name the reason.

skills.title: State the claim
skills.statement: You can state, in one sentence, the claim a source is making.
skills.teachingMove: Finish the sentence 'This source claims that...' before analyzing anything else.
checks: Write the claim of a passage in one sentence.
skills.transfer: State the claim of an unseen source from another genre.
skills.repair: Ask what the source wants you to believe or do by the end.

skills.title: Say what a cited source is doing
skills.statement: You can say whether a cited source supports, challenges, clarifies, or distinguishes a claim.
skills.teachingMove: For each citation, choose one of four jobs: prop, attack, refine, or split.
checks: Assign a job to a proof text and justify it in a sentence.
skills.transfer: Judge the role of a citation in an unseen argument.
skills.repair: Ask: is the claim stronger or weaker after this source, and why?

skills.title: Mark an objection
skills.statement: You can mark an objection and describe the pressure it puts on a claim.
skills.teachingMove: When the text pushes back, name what exactly it threatens: the claim, its reason, or its scope.
checks: Identify an objection and what it endangers.
skills.transfer: Locate the objection in an unseen philosophical passage.
skills.repair: Ask: what would be wrong if the first claim stood unchanged?

skills.title: Follow the response
skills.statement: You can follow how a response answers, narrows, or reframes an objection.
skills.teachingMove: Ask whether the response denies the objection, limits it, or accepts and adjusts the claim.
checks: Describe how a response handles its objection.
skills.transfer: Trace a response in an unseen sugya.
skills.repair: Compare the claim before and after the response and name what changed.

skills.title: Recognize an open tension
skills.statement: You can recognize when a source leaves a tension unresolved on purpose.
skills.teachingMove: Notice endings that stop without deciding; ask whether the openness is the point.
checks: Say whether a passage resolves, and if not, name the tension left standing.
skills.transfer: Judge resolution in an unseen aggadic or narrative passage.
skills.repair: Ask: did anyone here get the last word?

skills.title: Find the shared question
skills.statement: You can find the common question that two sources are both answering.

sourceContexts.ref: Hillel and Shammai on conversion, Shabbat 31a
Akiva and Ben Azzai on the great principle, Sifra Kedoshim

skills.teachingMove: Before contrasting, write the one question both sources are trying to answer.
checks: State the shared question behind two readings.
skills.transfer: Find the shared question across two unseen sources.
skills.repair: Ask what each source is a possible answer to, then find the overlap.

skills.title: Name where readings diverge
skills.statement: You can name the exact point where two readings part ways.

sourceContexts.ref: Rambam and Ramban on a mitzvah

skills.teachingMove: Lay the two answers in parallel and mark the first word where they no longer agree.
checks: Point to the specific point of divergence between two sources.
skills.transfer: Locate the divergence between two unseen readings.
skills.repair: State each answer in one line and compare them clause by clause.

skills.title: State each side at its strongest
skills.statement: You can give each side of a disagreement its strongest form before contrasting them.
skills.teachingMove: Argue each position as if you held it; only then place them next to each other.
checks: Give the strongest one-line case for each side.
skills.transfer: Steel-man both sides of an unseen dispute.
skills.repair: Ask what a smart person who held this view would say to defend it.

skills.title: Tell a real dispute from a scope difference
skills.statement: You can tell whether two sources truly disagree or are simply talking about different cases.
skills.teachingMove: Ask whether both sources are answering about the same case; different cases can hide a false conflict.
checks: Decide whether a pair is a real dispute or a scope difference, with a reason.
skills.transfer: Make the same call on an unseen pair.
skills.repair: Describe the exact case each source has in mind and check whether they match.

skills.title: Place a source in time and place
skills.statement: You can place a source in a rough time and place.

sourceContexts.ref: A Chassidic teaching and its rebbe's generation

skills.teachingMove: Attach every source to a rough era and setting before drawing conclusions from it.
checks: Give an approximate time and place for a source.
skills.transfer: Place an unfamiliar source within a century and a region.
skills.repair: Use the named people or language to estimate the era.

skills.title: Ask who made it and for whom
skills.statement: You can ask who produced a source and which community it addressed.
skills.teachingMove: Name the author and intended audience; a text written for scholars reads differently than one for a congregation.
checks: Name a plausible author and audience for a source.
skills.transfer: Infer author and audience for an unseen source.
skills.repair: Ask who would have needed this text and why.

skills.title: Let the genre set your expectations
skills.statement: You can use a source's genre to decide how it should and should not be read.

sourceContexts.ref: Aggadah vs. halakhah in one sugya

skills.teachingMove: Match the reading stance to the genre: a poem invites resonance, a code invites precision.
checks: State one thing this genre can and cannot be asked to deliver.
skills.transfer: Set correct expectations for an unseen genre.
skills.repair: Ask whether you are demanding a legal answer from a non-legal text or the reverse.

skills.title: Judge what evidence a source can give
skills.statement: You can judge what kind of evidence a source can and cannot provide.

sourceContexts.ref: Aggadic history vs. documentary evidence, Gittin 55b–56b
A Mussar teaching as guidance vs. as historical fact

skills.teachingMove: Ask what this source is good evidence for: a fact, a value, a memory, or a practice.
checks: State one claim this source supports and one it cannot.
skills.transfer: Judge the evidentiary reach of an unseen source.
skills.repair: Ask: if this were the only source, what could I responsibly conclude?

skills.title: Tell learning apart from a ruling
skills.statement: You can tell the difference between studying a halakhic source and receiving a ruling for yourself.

sourceContexts.ref: A sugya with multiple undecided views

skills.teachingMove: Separate two questions: what does this source say, and what should I do; the second needs more than reading.
checks: State what you have learned and what you have not yet been told to do.
skills.transfer: Draw the same line in an unseen halakhic source.
skills.repair: Ask: would a competent authority need to know more about me to answer this?

skills.title: Hold more than one view
skills.statement: You can hold more than one legitimate view without collapsing it into one.
skills.teachingMove: Report a disagreement as a live disagreement; resist the urge to declare a winner too early.
checks: Present two views fairly and say why both are kept.
skills.transfer: Preserve a dispute drawn from an unseen source.
skills.repair: Ask what is lost if only one of the views survives.

skills.title: Name the limits of what you learned
skills.statement: You can name the boundaries of what your reading has and has not established.

sourceContexts.ref: A philosophical claim with an open edge

skills.teachingMove: End each study with a sentence beginning 'What I have not settled is...'.
checks: State one thing your reading did not resolve.
skills.transfer: Name the limits after reading an unseen source.
skills.repair: Ask which of your conclusions you could not defend to a teacher.

skills.title: Know when to ask a person
skills.statement: You can recognize when a question needs a teacher or posek rather than a search.

sourceContexts.ref: A practical halakhic question of personal application
A sensitive interpretive or communal question

skills.teachingMove: Sort questions into 'I can read toward this' and 'this needs a person'; practice telling them apart.
checks: Given a question, decide whether to study it or bring it to a person, with a reason.
skills.transfer: Sort an unseen question correctly.
skills.repair: Ask whether being wrong here would affect a real decision or another person.

skills.title: Make a scaffolded first pass
skills.statement: You can make a supported first pass through an unfamiliar short source.
skills.teachingMove: Walk the source once for shape, once for signals, once for sense, with support ready at each pass.
checks: Produce a rough three-pass reading of a short unseen source.
skills.transfer: Do a first pass in a genre you have not practiced.
skills.repair: Slow to one pass for shape only, then rebuild.

skills.title: Map each line's job
skills.statement: You can label the job of each line in an unfamiliar passage before using a full translation.
skills.teachingMove: Give every line a one-word job before reaching for meaning; the map comes before the translation.
checks: Produce a line-by-line job map of an unseen passage.
skills.transfer: Map lines in a genre you did not practice.
skills.repair: Map only the lines you are sure of, then reason about the gaps.

skills.statement: You can use a translation to verify your reading rather than to replace it.
skills.title: Use translation to check, not to skip
skills.teachingMove: Commit to a read first, then open the translation only to confirm or correct it.
checks: Predict a line's meaning, then check it against a translation and note the gap.
skills.transfer: Do a predict-then-check pass in an unseen source.
skills.repair: If the translation surprised you, find the word you misjudged and add it to the word wall.

skills.title: Carry a reading move across genres
skills.statement: You can apply a reading move in a genre you never practiced it in.

sourceContexts.ref: Argument tracking moved from Gemara to Jewish thought
Case mapping moved from Mishnah to a Chassidic teaching

skills.teachingMove: Take a move you own in one genre and run it, out loud, in a genre that feels unrelated.
checks: Use one named skill in a genre where you have not used it before.
skills.transfer: Carry a move into a second unseen genre.
skills.repair: Name the move in the genre you know, then look for its equivalent in the new one.

skills.title: Ask a good question
skills.statement: You can ask a clear, answerable question about a source.
skills.teachingMove: Turn a vague 'I don't get it' into a question with a shape that could actually be answered.
checks: Write one answerable question about a source and say what a good answer would need.
skills.transfer: Ask a strong question about an unseen source.
skills.repair: Point to the exact word or line the question is about.

skills.title: Use a source tool on purpose
skills.statement: You can choose and use a dictionary, commentary, or cross-reference deliberately.

sourceContexts.ref: A commentary consulted to resolve a word

skills.teachingMove: Name what you are stuck on, then pick the one tool built to unstick it, instead of reaching randomly.
checks: State a difficulty and choose the right tool for it, with a reason.
skills.transfer: Pick the right tool for an unseen difficulty.
skills.repair: Ask whether your problem is a word, a claim, or a source, and match the tool to that.

skills.title: Record what you don't yet understand
skills.statement: You can record your open uncertainties honestly and in a form you can return to.

sourceContexts.ref: A study notebook entry after a sugya
A note after a philosophical passage

skills.teachingMove: End a session by writing the one thing you would want to reopen next time, specifically enough to act on.
checks: Write one useful, specific record of an open uncertainty.
skills.transfer: Record an open uncertainty after an unseen source.
skills.repair: Ask: if I came back in a week, would this note tell me where to start?

skills.title: Choose your next study move
skills.statement: You can choose your next study move and explain why it is next.

sourceContexts.ref: Choosing an elective direction after the foundation

skills.teachingMove: Given where you are, name the next move and the reason it beats the alternatives.
checks: Choose a next move and justify it against one other option.
skills.transfer: Make a defensible next-move choice from an unfamiliar position.
skills.repair: Ask what would most unlock the next thing you want to read.
